title: Lazarus, Come Out!
lead: The grave is not the limit of what God can do.
questions: Which matter in your life is so long dead that it already stinks, and are you ready to let Jesus come up to that grave?
Do you let yourself and others weep at gravesides, or do you demand a faith that forbids tears?
Who around you has already come out of the grave but still walks in the grave clothes of the past? How can you help unwrap them?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: The third fear in the section we are finishing today is the tomb being sealed. From Bethany, the “house of the poor,” a message reaches Jesus that is a model of prayer: “Lord, the one You love is sick.” No instructions and no “come at once.” Mary and Martha tell Him what is happening and leave the rest to His love. Yet Jesus stays where He is for two more days. A careful study of the text suggests that Lazarus may have died very early, perhaps before the message even reached Jesus. The story does not present His delay as the cause of death. Still, those who were waiting were allowed not to understand it, and so are we.

Martha and Mary greet the Savior with the same sentence: “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” This is what the grief of believers sounds like – and Jesus never once rebukes it. To Martha, who understands the resurrection “at the last day,” He doesn’t correct her doctrine. He simply moves the emphasis from a distant “then” to the “now” standing in front of her: “I am the resurrection and the life… Do you believe this?” Hope is not a calendar of end-time events; it is a Person standing beside you. In this story we also find one of the shortest verses in the Bible: “Jesus wept.” The Greeks taught that you could recognize a god by his imperturbability. The Gospel, however, shows God weeping in a cemetery, even though He knows better than anyone what is about to happen. The hope of the resurrection doesn’t take away the right to grieve – it helps us go through grief.

At the tomb Martha still protests: “By now he stinks… It has already been four days.” After so long, it is certain that Lazarus is not alive. But God is not limited by anything. For the first time in this Gospel, Jesus prays aloud, addressing the Most High as “Father,” and then calls out: “Lazarus, come out!” The dead man comes out, still wrapped in strips of linen, and then comes the final command, addressed to the people: “Unwrap him and let him go.” God performed the miracle, and the unwrapping He left to the community. People awakened by Jesus come out of their graves still wrapped in the grave clothes of the past. A church that only remembers what someone smells like leaves the raised still bound.

The thematic section we are finishing today names three fears: the boat is sinking, the bread runs out, the tomb is sealed. We have already seen the storm and the hunger. Today the Gospel leads us up to the third, final wall, beyond which, humanly speaking, there is nothing. The story takes place in Bethany, a village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, a brisk fifteen-minute walk from Jerusalem. The name itself says a lot: Bethany most likely means “house of the poor.” There Jesus had a home in the warmest sense of the word: a family of friends, Martha, Mary and Lazarus, whom He visited, with whom He ate and rested. It is from there that the news comes that everyone who loves someone dreads.

sections.heading: The One You Love Is Sick
paragraphs: The sisters’ message is a model of prayer in time of need: “Lord, the one You love is sick.” No request, no instructions, no “come at once.” The sisters don’t tell Jesus what to do. They tell Him what is happening and leave the rest to His love. That makes what follows hit all the harder: Jesus “stayed where He was for two days.” Two days of silence for a household waiting to be rescued. For centuries a charge has hung over this delay: He let His friend die so the miracle would be bigger. The chronology of the story suggests that Lazarus may have died very early, perhaps even before the message reached Jesus. So we cannot assume that Christ’s delay had any effect at all on Lazarus’s death. To the question of why He waited at all, the Savior answers: “For your sake… so that you may believe.” There are things God does in a rhythm that makes no sense to those who are waiting. This story honestly shows that we are allowed not to understand. Whether we understand it later or never, we will still be loved by Him.

Jesus is going to Judea, where people had just tried to stone Him. The disciples protest, and Thomas closes the discussion with a sentence that is at once heroic and without illusions: “Let us also go, so that we may die with Him.” In everyone’s eyes, this trip to Bethany was a march toward death. And in fact it was: it is the raising of Lazarus that will make the cup overflow and set in motion the decision to kill Jesus. The Teacher goes to wake His friend, knowing He will pay the highest price for it.

sections.heading: If You Had Been Here
paragraphs: Martha goes out to meet Him, and Mary stays at home. Both, each in her own time, will speak the identical sentence: “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” This is what the grief of believers sounds like: not blasphemy, not unbelief, just a painful “if only” addressed to a God who could have prevented it and didn’t. Jesus accepts that sentence twice and never once rebukes it. The conversation with Martha becomes one of the most important dialogues in the Gospel. Martha’s theology is entirely correct: “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.” She confesses exactly what she was taught in the best school of thinking about the future. Jesus doesn’t correct her confession. He simply moves the emphasis from a distant “then” to the “now” standing in front of her: “I am the resurrection and the life.” He doesn’t announce a resurrection; He says that He is it. The whole series of “I am” sayings in this Gospel, from the bread of life to the gate and the shepherd, reaches its climax here, and not in a lecture hall but by the side of the road, in front of a weeping woman. Then comes the question that leaps from the abstract to the concrete: “Do you believe this?” Not “Do you affirm this thesis?” but: Do you trust Me, here, over your brother’s fresh grave? Christian hope is not a calendar of end-time events. It is a Person who stands beside you when the calendar has stopped promising anything.

sections.heading: Jesus Wept
paragraphs: Then Mary comes with the same “if You had been here,” and behind her the weeping mourners. And something happens that the Greek text describes in stronger words than translations convey. Jesus “was deeply moved in spirit”: the verb John uses denotes violent agitation with a note of anger; in classical Greek it could even describe the snorting of a horse. At His friend’s grave Jesus is not melancholy. He is shaken and angry. That anger, however, is aimed not at people but at death itself: the intruder that ravages God’s world and the homes of His friends. At this point in the story we also find one of the shortest verses in the Bible: “Jesus wept.” In part of the Greek philosophical tradition, the idea of divine imperturbability, apatheia, was an important ideal. Yet the Gospel shows God standing in a cemetery, weeping. And notice the strangest thing of all: He weeps knowing that in five minutes Lazarus will walk out of the tomb. That knowledge doesn’t cancel the tears. This is the answer for everyone who has ever been told that “real faith doesn’t cry, because we’ll see each other in heaven.” Jesus knew the ending better than anyone, and yet He wept with those who wept. The hope of the resurrection doesn’t take away the right to grieve – it helps us go through grief without being lost in it.

sections.heading: Take Away the Stone
paragraphs: Lazarus’s tomb was a natural cave or a chamber cut in the rock, with shelves for the bodies, closed with a heavy stone. That is what the burial places of better-off families looked like at the time. In front of this sealed cave the final test plays out. Jesus orders the stone to be rolled away, and Martha, the same Martha who has just confessed her faith, protests: “Lord, by now he stinks… It has already been four days.” This underlines that there was no doubt at all about Lazarus’s death. Martha is protecting Jesus from embarrassment and herself from one last disappointment. Her “by now he stinks” is the voice of every one of us over matters that died so long ago that it no longer seems decent to pray about them. Jesus answers with a question: “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” Right after that He does something He has never done before in this Gospel – He prays aloud, addressing the Almighty: “Father.” The first ten chapters of this book spoke of the Father in the third person. The first prayer spoken aloud to Him comes in a cemetery, beside an open grave, before witnesses, “so they may believe that You sent Me.” After this short conversation with the Most High, Jesus calls toward the dark opening: “Lazarus, come out!”

sections.heading: Unwrap Him
paragraphs: “The man who had been dead came out.” The evangelist reports it as calmly as if he were describing someone stepping out of the house. He also adds a detail: Lazarus comes out with his hands and feet bound in strips of linen and his face hidden under a cloth. Alive, but still wrapped in death. Then Jesus gives the last command of this story, addressed not to Lazarus but to the onlookers: “Unwrap him and let him go.” God performed the miracle, and the unwrapping He left to people. That sentence should hang over the door of every church. People come out of graves we had already buried them in – out of addiction, out of unbelief, out of old failures, out of our own judgment. Very often they still have the strips of linen on them: they smell of the past, they are awkward, bound up in what used to be. The community’s role is not to check whether they are really alive. It is to unwrap them, that is, to patiently remove from a person what they were buried in, until they can walk. A church that only remembers what someone used to smell like leaves the raised still in their grave clothes.

It’s also worth seeing what this story set in motion. John goes on to say that many of the mourners believed, while the council of priests decided to kill Jesus, and not only Him. “So the chief priests made plans to kill Lazarus as well, for on account of him many of the Jews were deserting them and believing in Jesus.” That decision says something important about the nature of testimony. Lazarus dead bothered no one; Lazarus alive became unbearable, even though the Gospel doesn’t quote a single word he said. He didn’t preach sermons. He only lived, ate dinners and could be touched – that was enough for people to come to believe. The hardest argument for Christianity to refute has never been rhetoric. It has been people who plainly came out of the grave.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: If today you are standing beside something that has died, this story tells you three things. First: God’s silence is not His absence. Two days of silence didn’t mean Jesus had stopped loving the people of the household in Bethany. God often works in ways we don’t understand while they are happening. It is worth stressing that we are allowed to voice that lack of understanding out loud, as Martha and Mary did. Second: you are allowed to weep. The One who knows the ending of every story stood in a cemetery and wept; a faith that forbids tears is not the faith of Jesus. Third: the fact that something or someone has begun to stink is no obstacle for God. The line past which it “no longer seems decent” to hope is the limit of our imagination, not of His power. The question Jesus asked Martha is addressed today to each of us: “I am the resurrection and the life… Do you believe this?”
